title: Ellipses from quadratic forms
objectives: Read the shape of a quadratic form from its eigenvalues.
Find the axes of $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = c$ and of a risk ellipse.

screens.title: A curve from a matrix
screens.prose: Take $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 4x^2 + y^2$. The curve is every point where this equals 1. P rides the curve: drag it round.
screens.question: How far from the origin does the curve cross the positive $x$-axis?

hints.text: Drag P down onto the $x$-axis and read its $x$.
On the $x$-axis, $y = 0$. Solve $4x^2 = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $y = 0$ and solve $4x^2 = 1$.

byKey.lambda: You read the 4 in the matrix as the distance. It multiplies $x^2$, so the curve is pulled in, not pushed out.
byKey.inverse: You solved $4x = 1$. The form has $x^2$, so take a square root: $x = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

explain.text: On the axis $4x^2 = 1$, so the curve crosses at $x = \tfrac{1}{2}$, and at $y = 1$ on the other axis. The curve is an ellipse. The bigger entry, 4, gave the shorter half-width.

screens.title: Two eigenvalues and a turn
screens.prose: Now $\mathbf{A}$ has eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ along $\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\lambda_2$ along $\mathbf{q}_2$. The angle turns both eigenvectors together. The two segments run from the centre to the curve along $\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$. Slide all three.
screens.question: Take $\lambda_1$ from 1 to 4. What happens to the half-axis along $\mathbf{q}_1$?

options.why: You expected the length to follow $\lambda$ down in step. The caption reads 1.00, then 0.50: a half.
You read a bigger eigenvalue as a longer axis. A bigger $\lambda$ makes the form climb faster, so the curve sits closer in.

options.text: It turns to a new direction
options.why: You may have mixed the sliders. Only the angle turns the axes; $\lambda_1$ changes a length.

hints.text: Set the angle anywhere, then watch the first half-axis as $\lambda_1$ goes from 1 to 4.

feedback.correct: Four times the eigenvalue, half the length: the half-axis is $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first half-axis in the caption at $\lambda_1 = 1$ and at $\lambda_1 = 4$.

explain.text: The caption went from 1.00 to 0.50: the half-axis is $1/\sqrt{\lambda_1}$. The angle slider turned the ellipse without changing its shape. Its axes always lie along the eigenvectors.

screens.title: Principal axes
screens.prose: For $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, eigenvalue 3 goes with $(1, 1)$ and eigenvalue 1 with $(1, -1)$. The ellipse $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 1$ has its **principal axes** along them. Drag P round to measure.

derive.caption: Distance from the centre to P: {{fixed(hypot(P.x, P.y), 3)}}

screens.question: How long is the half-axis along $(1, 1)$?

hints.text: Drag P onto the dashed line $y = x$ and read the distance.
The half-axis is $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$ for the eigenvalue of that direction.
Along $(1, 1)$, $\lambda = 3$, so the half-axis is $1/\sqrt{3} \approx 0.577$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the eigenvalue for $(1, 1)$ and take $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$.

byKey.lambda: You used the eigenvalue itself as the length. The half-axis is $1/\sqrt{3}$.
byKey.inverse: You took $1/\lambda$. The form is quadratic, so the length is $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$.
byKey.root: You took $\sqrt{3}$. A bigger eigenvalue gives a shorter axis: $1/\sqrt{3}$.
byKey.other: That is the long half-axis, along $(1, -1)$ with $\lambda = 1$. Measure along $(1, 1)$.

explain.text: Along $(1, 1)$ the distance was smallest, $1/\sqrt{3} \approx 0.577$. Along $(1, -1)$ it was largest, $1/\sqrt{1} = 1$. The principal axes are the eigenvectors, and the half-axes are $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$.

screens.title: Which axis is long
screens.prose: Now $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}5&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix}$, with eigenvalue 8 along $(1, 1)$ and 2 along $(1, -1)$. The ellipse $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 1$ is hidden; the dashed lines are its axes.
screens.question: Along which direction is the long axis, and how long is its half?

options.why: You matched the long axis to the big eigenvalue. $1/\sqrt{8}$ is the short half-axis.
You read the eigenvalue as a length. Lengths are $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$, so big $\lambda$ means short.
Right direction, but you took $1/\lambda$. The half-axis is $1/\sqrt{2}$.

hints.text: Which eigenvalue makes $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$ larger?
The smaller eigenvalue, 2, goes with $(1, -1)$.
Long half-axis: $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71$ along $(1, -1)$.

feedback.correct: The smaller eigenvalue gives the longer axis: $1/\sqrt{2}$ along $(1, -1)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$ for both eigenvalues.

explain.text: Half-axes are $1/\sqrt{8} \approx 0.35$ along $(1, 1)$ and $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71$ along $(1, -1)$. The long axis is twice the short one, since $\sqrt{8/2} = 2$. The form climbs slowest along the long axis.

screens.title: A higher level
screens.prose: Back to $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. The inner curve is $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 1$. The outer curve, hidden for now, is $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 9$.
screens.question: Where does $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 9$ cross the positive $x$-axis?

hints.text: On the $x$-axis, $y = 0$.
Solve $4x^2 = 9$.
$x^2 = \tfrac{9}{4}$, so $x = \tfrac{3}{2}$: three times the level-1 half-axis.

feedback.correct: $x = \tfrac{3}{2}$: the level 9 scales every half-axis by $\sqrt{9} = 3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $y = 0$ and solve $4x^2 = 9$.

byKey.no-c: That is the crossing at level 1. At level 9, solve $4x^2 = 9$.
byKey.times9: You multiplied the half-axis 0.5 by 9. Lengths scale by $\sqrt{9} = 3$.
byKey.over4: You solved $4x = 9$. The form has $x^2$: take a square root.

explain.text: $4x^2 = 9$ gives $x = 1.5$, three times the 0.5 at level 1. In general $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = c$ has half-axes $\sqrt{c/\lambda}$. The same shape, scaled by $\sqrt{c}$.

screens.title: Eigenvalues of both signs
screens.prose: $\mathbf{T} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue 3 along $(1, 1)$ and $-1$ along $(1, -1)$. The curve $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{T}\mathbf{x} = 1$ is hidden; the dashed lines are the eigen-directions.
screens.question: What does $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{T}\mathbf{x} = 1$ look like?

options.text: Two curves that cross $(1, 1)$'s line at distance $1/\sqrt{3}$ and never meet $(1, -1)$'s line

options.why: You dropped the sign of $-1$. Along $(1, -1)$ the form is $-|\mathbf{x}|^2$, which never reaches 1.
Parallel lines come from an eigenvalue of 0. Here it is $-1$, not 0.
You may have looked only along $(1, -1)$. Along $(1, 1)$ the form is $3|\mathbf{x}|^2$, which does reach 1.

hints.text: Along each eigen-direction, $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{T}\mathbf{x} = \lambda|\mathbf{x}|^2$. Which directions can reach 1?
Along $(1, -1)$, $\lambda = -1$, so the form is negative there.
The curve meets the $(1, 1)$ line at $1/\sqrt{3}$ and bends away from the $(1, -1)$ line forever: a hyperbola.

feedback.correct: A hyperbola: the level set of a saddle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask, direction by direction, whether $\lambda|\mathbf{x}|^2$ can equal 1.

explain.text: Along $(1, 1)$, $3|\mathbf{x}|^2 = 1$ at distance $1/\sqrt{3}$. Along $(1, -1)$ the form is never positive, so the curve never gets there. Opposite-sign eigenvalues give a hyperbola, the contour of a saddle.

screens.title: Reading the length
screens.prose: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}0.25&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 0.25x^2 + y^2$. The ellipse where it equals 1 is hidden. It passes through $(0, 1)$.
screens.question: Drag P to where the ellipse crosses the positive $x$-axis.

hints.text: On the $x$-axis, $y = 0$, so solve $0.25x^2 = 1$.

byKey.lambda: You put P at 0.25, reading the eigenvalue as the length. A small eigenvalue gives a long axis: $1/\sqrt{0.25} = 2$.
byKey.root: You took $\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$. The length is the reciprocal of that: $1/\sqrt{0.25} = 2$.
byKey.inverse: You took $1/0.25 = 4$. That is $x^2$; the crossing is its square root, 2.
byKey.P: P is not on the crossing yet. Solve $0.25x^2 = 1$.

explain.text: $0.25x^2 = 1$ gives $x^2 = 4$ and $x = 2$. The eigenvalue 0.25 is small, so the form climbs slowly and the curve reaches far out. Half-axis $= 1/\sqrt{\lambda}$, never $\lambda$.

screens.title: Why one over root lambda
screens.prose: Let $\mathbf{q}$ be a unit eigenvector of symmetric $\mathbf{A}$, with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q} = \lambda\mathbf{q}$ and $\lambda > 0$. Walk out from the centre along $\mathbf{q}$ until $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 1$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Put $\mathbf{x} = t\mathbf{q}$ with $t > 0$, a point along $\mathbf{q}$
$\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = t^2\,\mathbf{q}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}$, taking the number $t$ out twice

hints.text: Start by naming the point on the line through $\mathbf{q}$.
Use the eigenvector equation before the unit length.
Point, pull out $t$, eigenvector, unit length, solve.

feedback.correct: Along an eigenvector the form is just $\lambda t^2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name the point first, then simplify $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ one fact at a time.

byKey.unit: $\mathbf{q}^T\mathbf{q}$ only appears after $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}$ is replaced by $\lambda\mathbf{q}$. Put the eigenvector line first.
byKey.solve: Solving needs the form reduced to $\lambda t^2$. It comes last.

explain.text: Along $\mathbf{q}$ the form is $\lambda t^2$, so it reaches 1 at $t = 1/\sqrt{\lambda}$. At level $c$ it is $\sqrt{c/\lambda}$. With $\lambda \le 0$ there is no solution: that direction never reaches the curve.

screens.title: Risk ellipses
screens.prose: The curve $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = c$ has axes along the eigenvectors and half-axes $\sqrt{c/\lambda_i}$. For a covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, the ellipse $\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} = c$ is a **confidence region** of a bivariate normal. $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ has the same eigenvectors, with eigenvalues $1/\lambda_i$.
screens.question: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ has eigenvalues 9 and 1. What are the half-axes of $\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} = 1$?

options.why: You used the eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ in $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$. The matrix in the form is $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$, with eigenvalues $\tfrac{1}{9}$ and 1.
You read variances as lengths. Lengths are standard deviations: $\sqrt{9} = 3$.
You used the eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ as lengths. Take $1/\sqrt{1/9} = 3$.

hints.text: The eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ are $\tfrac{1}{9}$ and 1. Apply $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$, then take $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$.

explain.text: For $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ the half-axes are $\sqrt{c\,\lambda_i(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}$: standard deviations along each eigen-portfolio. So the long axis of a risk ellipse points along the largest-variance direction of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.

screens.title: The shape of a return cloud
screens.prose: Forty days of returns for two stocks, in %. Their $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}2&1.6\\1.6&2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue 3.6 along $(1, 1)$ and 0.4 along $(1, -1)$. The line is the principal direction. The risk ellipses $\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} = c$ wrap the cloud.
screens.question: How many times longer is a risk ellipse's long axis than its short axis?

hints.text: The half-axes of $\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} = c$ are $\sqrt{c\,\lambda_i}$, with $\lambda_i$ the eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
The $c$ cancels in the ratio.

feedback.correct: 3: the cloud is three times as long along $(1, 1)$ as across it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the two half-axes $\sqrt{c\,\lambda_i}$.

byKey.variance: You divided the variances. Lengths are standard deviations: $\sqrt{9} = 3$.
byKey.flip: You divided short by long. The long axis is along $(1, 1)$, the larger eigenvalue.
byKey.eig-diff: You subtracted the eigenvalues. The axes compare as a ratio of square roots.

explain.text: Standard deviations along the axes are $\sqrt{3.6} \approx 1.90$ and $\sqrt{0.4} \approx 0.63$, a ratio of 3. The cloud runs along $(1, 1)$, the stocks moving together. PCA finds this direction from the data alone.

ideas: $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = 1$, with positive eigenvalues, is an ellipse whose axes lie along the eigenvectors.
The half-axis along $\mathbf{q}_i$ is $1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}$: a big eigenvalue means a short axis. Opposite signs give a hyperbola.
For a covariance matrix, $\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} = c$ has half-axes $\sqrt{c\,\lambda_i}$: its long axis follows the largest variance.

formula.name: Half-axes of a quadratic form
formula.note: For $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ the eigenvalues invert, so the half-axes are $\sqrt{c\,\lambda_i(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}$.

summary.trap: The half-axis is $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$, not $\lambda$: $0.25x^2 + y^2 = 1$ reaches $x = 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$ for each eigenvalue and take the larger.

byKey.short: That is $1/\sqrt{9}$, the short half-axis. The smaller eigenvalue gives the long one.
byKey.lambda: You read the eigenvalue as a length. Lengths are $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$.

explain.text: Half-axes are $1/\sqrt{9} = \tfrac{1}{3}$ along $x$ and $1/\sqrt{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}$ along $y$. The long one is 0.5.

options.why: You paired the long axis with the big eigenvalue. $\tfrac{1}{2}$ is the short half-axis.
You read the diagonal entry 3 as an eigenvalue. The off-diagonal 1 turns the axes to the diagonals.
Right direction, but the length is $1/\sqrt{2}$, not the eigenvalue.

feedback.correct: The smaller eigenvalue, 2, gives the long half-axis $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The long axis goes with the smaller eigenvalue.

explain.text: Half-axes are $1/\sqrt{4} = 0.5$ along $(1, 1)$ and $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71$ along $(1, -1)$. The ellipse is stretched along $(1, -1)$.

options.why: You treated the 0 like a 1. The form is $x^2$ alone; $y$ is free.
You fixed $y = 0$. The form ignores $y$, so every $y$ works.

options.text: A long ellipse with half-axes 1 and 100
options.why: You took a zero eigenvalue as a small one. $1/\sqrt{0}$ is not a number: the curve never closes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ and see which variable is missing.

explain.text: $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = x^2$, so the curve is $x = \pm 1$ for any $y$. A zero eigenvalue stretches that axis to infinity: the level set of a trough.

quiz.question: How long is the long half-axis of $\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} = 1$?

feedback.correct: 2, the standard deviation of the first return.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Invert $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ first, then take $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$.

byKey.sigma: You used $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ in place of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$: $1/\sqrt{4}$. The form uses the inverse, so the length is $\sqrt{4}$.
byKey.variance: You used the variance as the length. The half-axis is its square root, 2.

explain.text: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{1}{4}&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so the curve is $\tfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1$. It crosses the $x$-axis at 2, one standard deviation. The long axis lies along the larger variance.
